clue.text: Newspaper employees blocking newspaper? Just a little

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits inside it, so the employees go inside the paper

blocks.note: the Financial Times, the pink British business daily
a rag is a dismissive word for a newspaper
workers, staff

explanation.surface: A question about journalists crowding out a rival paper, answered with a modest shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'newspaper's are used: the scornful word for a paper sits with the staff inside the pink British business daily's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragment is a small broken piece, only a tiny portion of some whole.

clue.text: Short film sequences giving one various impressions

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
dents are hollows impressed into a surface

explanation.surface: An impressionist's showreel of brief clips, each doing a different voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressions' suggests mimicry, but here it means physical marks pressed into something.
explanation.definitionFit: Idents are brief station-identification clips that broadcasters run between programmes.

clue.text: Shabby party ready to roll?

blocks.note: a do is an informal word for a party
geared up, prepared to get going

explanation.surface: A tired-looking party that is nonetheless raring to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog-eared book has worn, turned-down page corners, so it looks worn and tatty.

clue.text: Got ready to listen, perhaps, having received note

indicators.note: a word that has received something holds it inside, so the musical letter goes within

blocks.note: having ears, and so equipped for listening
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: Someone pricking up their ears on being handed a message.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word at the start; 'perhaps' warns that EARED is only one way to be ready to listen.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to obtain something as a reward, so earned can stand for acquired or received.

clue.text: Active gear ripped or lasted

indicators.note: ripped means torn apart, so the words are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Sportswear that either tore or survived the workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripped' also hints at a muscular gym-goer, adding to the fitness picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Leotards are close-fitting garments worn for dance, gymnastics and exercise, so they are kit for physical activity.

clue.text: Medical injury? Put under protection, avoiding A & E

indicators.note: avoiding means keeping clear of, so those two letters are left out

blocks.note: to insulate is to wrap in a protective layer
the letters A and E, also the hospital Accident and Emergency department

explanation.surface: A medical mishap where a patient was wrapped up but kept out of Accident and Emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: A & E is the British name for a hospital emergency department; here it is simply the letters A and E.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine an insult is a technical term for damage or trauma inflicted on the body or an organ.

clue.text: Note risk when playing at the crease?

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are played about with and moved around

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricketer noticing the danger of batting.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the crease is the line the batter stands at; the batter facing the bowler is said to be on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricketer on strike is the one currently facing the bowling, standing ready at the crease.

clue.text: Be enthusiastic about Democrat leading US state transmission

indicators.note: about means around, so the enthusiasm word wraps the other pieces

blocks.note: to rave about something is to praise it wildly
D is the abbreviation for Democrat
a state in the American Midwest

explanation.surface: Political excitement about a Democrat winning an American state, broadcast to all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' simply puts D before IOWA inside the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio waves are electromagnetic signals used to broadcast sound and data, so they carry a transmission.

clue.text: Contribution to run in the last inning?

indicators.note: a contribution is a part of the whole, so the answer is a part of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A baseball player scoring a run late in the game.
explanation.walkthrough: In baseball a regulation game has nine innings, hence the question mark on the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard baseball game ends after nine innings, so the ninth is normally the final one.

clue.text: Present: something received by the recipient

indicators.note: what is received is held inside, so the answer sits within the next words

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A gift defined as whatever arrives with the person it is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, matching the surface; it means in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'here' at a roll call shows you are in attendance, the adjectival sense of present.

clue.text: Biscuit for one turned over in the midst of turning out

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the two letters run backwards
in the midst of means surrounded by, so the short piece goes inside
out here means wrong or disordered, so the combined letters are rearranged

blocks.note: e.g., for example, as in 'for one'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A biscuit flipped over while being tipped out of the packet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links definition to wordplay; 'one' alone is EG, an example. A gingernut is a hard British ginger biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A gingernut is a crunchy ginger-flavoured cookie, a familiar type of British biscuit.

clue.text: Complete club ousting leader

indicators.note: the leader is thrown out, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: a putter is a golf club used on the green

explanation.surface: A sports club or society that has finished by deposing its chairman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a society, but it is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter is an adjective meaning total or absolute, as in utter nonsense.

clue.text: Completely ousting leader of college

indicators.note: removing the leader means dropping the opening letter

blocks.note: a hall is a college or residence at a university

explanation.surface: A college staging a total coup against its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader of college' looks like a single letter C, but 'ousting leader' is the deletion and college is the word acted on.
explanation.definitionFit: All can be an adverb meaning entirely or wholly, as in all alone.

clue.text: Road movie? I had little hesitation after years at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
I'd is the contraction of I had
er, a short sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A sailor, after years at sea, barely hesitating before a road trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the jumbled years first; the question mark marks the definition as a play on the film genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy Rider is the 1969 motorcycle film with Peter Fonda, the classic of the road-trip genre.

clue.text: Time of disturbance moved forward for small group

indicators.note: moved forward means a letter shifts to the front of its word

blocks.note: points to the letter for time within the next word, the letter that moves
a riot is a violent public disturbance

explanation.surface: The hour of a public disorder brought forward for a small gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time of disturbance' is the T within the second word, which shifts from the end to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A trio is a set of three, whether musicians or people, so a small grouping.

clue.text: Drink a lot of salt water?

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: tears are drops of salty water from the eyes

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether to drink seawater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt water' suggests the sea, but it is a teardrop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is an everyday hot beverage made from infused leaves.

clue.text: Nobleman, mostly bent, importing diamonds to European country

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is lost
importing means bringing in, so the shortened word takes in the other pieces

blocks.note: curved like an arch
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds
the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A crooked aristocrat smuggling gems into a European country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' hints at dishonesty in the surface but means curved. 'to' joins diamonds and the country, which both go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An archduke is a high-ranking prince, a title held chiefly by Habsburg royalty in Austria.

clue.text: Puts down record after ingesting medicines? On the contrary

indicators.note: ingesting means swallowing, so one piece takes the other inside it
on the contrary reverses who swallows whom, so the medicines take in the record

blocks.note: measured amounts of medicine
an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A record being swallowed along with some pills.
explanation.walkthrough: As written, the record swallows the medicines; the closing phrase swaps the roles.
explanation.definitionFit: To depose is to remove a ruler from power, which is to put them down or topple them.

clue.text: Instruction to give 'em tonic?

blocks.note: surface reading: an order to hand out a tonic drink to some people
setter's reading: the drink's name read as a command someone gives, asking to be lifted

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a drink that revives you and, read literally, a request to be collected or lifted.
explanation.definitionFit: A pick-me-up is a restorative drink or tonic, and its name is itself phrased as a command.

clue.text: Pushchair getting wave at end of street

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street
a roller is a long heavy sea wave

explanation.surface: A parent with a buggy being waved at at the end of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At end of' puts the wave after the street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroller is the usual American word for a baby buggy, the British pushchair.

clue.text: Mischievous character shown by German soccer team?

blocks.note: first meaning: a small impish sprite from folklore
second meaning: German for eleven, the number in a football side

explanation.surface: A prankster revealed by the antics of a German football side.
explanation.walkthrough: A football team is an eleven, and the German word for eleven is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves are playful, trouble-making little folk in legend; the German numeral for eleven is spelt the same.

clue.text: Border row? French willing to be above that

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for French
on, as in game or up for something
a tier is one row of seats or layers

explanation.surface: A dispute over a border, with the French keen to rise above it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'to be above that' puts the French and willing pieces over the row; 'row' suggests a quarrel but means a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A frontier is the boundary line between two countries.

clue.text: Move over the sea, caught in a lot of foam

indicators.note: a lot of means most of, so the final letter is cut
something caught in a thing is trapped inside it

blocks.note: C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
soapy froth

explanation.surface: A boat skimming the waves, trapped in heaps of sea foam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' alone is the cricket abbreviation; 'in' places it inside the shortened foam.
explanation.definitionFit: To scud is to move fast and smoothly, used of ships running before the wind and clouds racing.

clue.text: Magistrate with money giving ride to daughter in car

indicators.note: giving someone a ride means carrying them inside, so the letter goes within

blocks.note: the doge was the chief magistrate of Venice or Genoa
M is the abbreviation for money
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A wealthy official giving his daughter a lift in his car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ride' fits the fairground answer, but the definition is just the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodgem is a small electric bumper car at a funfair, driven to bump into others.

clue.text: Smoked item cooked in garlic oil

indicators.note: cooked means prepared or mixed together, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A kitchen recipe for something smoked, prepared in garlic-flavoured oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoked' suggests smoked food, but it is something one smokes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarillo is a small thin cigar, an item a smoker smokes.

clue.text: Good to stir up complaint

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to rouse is to stir or wake

explanation.surface: Advice that it is right to stoke a grievance.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouse is an informal word for a grumble or gripe.

clue.text: Smooth support, a tiny bit short

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: a leg supports a table or chair
taken as written
a tot is a small amount, especially of spirits

explanation.surface: A support or brace that is a fraction too short to be level.
explanation.definitionFit: Legato is the musical direction to play notes smoothly and connected, without breaks.

clue.text: Historic leader disengaged from area

blocks.note: off, as in no longer attached to or away from
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A former ruler who has withdrawn from a region.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was an eighth-century English king of Mercia, famous for Offa's Dyke on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, so he is a ruler from the distant past.

clue.text: Good to hug a tree

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap the arms around, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: OK means acceptable, all right
taken as written

explanation.surface: Praise for tree-hugging.
explanation.definitionFit: The oak is a large, long-lived hardwood species bearing acorns.

clue.text: Fellow gave assistance after one dropped out tired

indicators.note: dropped out means removed, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
helped
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A helper who gave up exhausted after a colleague quit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the shortened assistance word behind the fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Faded can describe something worn out, jaded or past its best.

clue.text: Idiot might, swapping openings, work on the sly

indicators.note: the two words exchange their first letters with each other

blocks.note: a loon is a foolish or crazy person
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that a fool may change jobs to work secretly.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters are swapped on paper, not by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To moonlight is to hold a second job secretly, usually at night and undeclared.

clue.text: Leg joint to irk, run being cancelled

indicators.note: something cancelled is struck out, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: to rankle is to annoy persistently
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: An injured joint that would annoy a runner whose race was called off.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomically this is the hinge between foot and shin, the commonest joint in the lower limb to sprain.

clue.text: Reveal the woman involved in articles from France and England

indicators.note: involved in means caught up inside, so the woman sits between the others

blocks.note: un is a French indefinite article
the pronoun for a woman
England's articles, the indefinite a and the definite the

explanation.surface: A woman caught up in some Anglo-French dealings is exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' serves both countries: one French article, then both English ones, with the woman placed among them.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsheathe is to draw a blade from its scabbard, bringing it out into view.
